READING

**What each course must do**

The February test has three parts: fourteen hours a week of originated speech, with commissioned content no more than half of that originated total, and thirty contributors on the register.

On the contributor count both courses pass easily. Marsh Head holds 34 and commissioned producers do not reduce that number, so even with natural attrition there is a four-person buffer against the thirty threshold under either course.

On the commissioned-production ratio, ELSWICK adds six commissioned hours to the nine already carried, producing a total of fifteen hours with six commissioned. Six-fifteenths is forty percent, comfortably inside the fifty-percent ceiling. The arithmetic here causes no concern.

The decisive variable is whether the fourteen-hour floor is cleared by the end of February 2027.

---

**The timeline pressure on CRANMOOR**

A coordinator in post from 1 October 2026 has, at most, five months before the four-week measurement window opens in late January 2027. The station's own planning note says fourteen hours needs about fifteen more active contributors. In the whole of 2025 — twelve months, no coordinator — nine were added. That is 0.75 per month organically.

A coordinator can reasonably be expected to improve on that, perhaps substantially. But to recruit fifteen contributors who are active enough to be generating scheduled output before the measurement window closes, the station would need roughly three new contributing voices a month from a standing start. That is a rate four times the unassisted pace. Even a doubled rate — which would be a strong performance — yields perhaps nine or ten new contributors in the window, and with them perhaps two or three additional hours a week. That moves the dial from nine toward eleven or twelve, not to fourteen.

There is also the question of what "building the hours out of the roster" means in practice. New contributors rarely move straight to regular output; there is usually an onboarding lag of several weeks. The February window is unforgiving on timing as well as on numbers.

CRANMOOR is a better long-term design. The hours, once built, cost nothing to repeat, and the coordinator works the register simultaneously, directly addressing the slide from 41 to 34. These are real strategic advantages. But they are advantages that materialise only if the station clears February, and the probability of doing so on this timetable, against this recruitment history, is low enough to constitute a genuine strategic risk.

---

**What happens if CRANMOOR misses February**

If the station is short of the mark at the February assessment it is remeasured on 31 August 2027. Local Voice payment starts only when it clears. The four-year period still runs from 1 April 2027, so any months of delay reduce total receipts from the scheme.

More pressingly, from 1 April 2027 the current £71,000 grant ends. With no Local Voice in payment and fixed costs of £58,000 a year plus the coordinator at £21,000, the station is burning through roughly £6,600 a month with no grant income. Four months to the August reassessment costs around £26,000 from a £62,000 reserve — leaving the reserve at roughly £36,000, which is below a six-month cost buffer. And that assumes the August assessment is passed first time. If the contributor-led growth strategy was not delivering by February it may not have delivered enough by August either.

The reserve is the station's only safety net. Halving it in a worst-case CRANMOOR scenario is a risk the organisation may not be positioned to recover from quickly, particularly since fixed costs — transmission, premises, licence at £58,000 — do not compress.

---

**The ELSWICK position**

ELSWICK delivers fifteen hours a week against a fourteen-hour threshold, with six of those hours commissioned, well inside the fifty-percent rule. It costs £20,280 a year, within the board's £22,000 cap. The Halverston rate is held at £65 to the end of 2026. The rolling twelve-month contract starting 5 October 2026 is in place before the measurement window and buys the compliance position on contract rather than on hope.

If Local Voice comes in from 1 April 2027 at £96,000, the station's annual position is: £96,000 less £58,000 fixed costs, less £20,280 Halverston, leaving a surplus of approximately £17,700. That is a sound operating position.

The weaknesses of ELSWICK are real. Halverston's rate after December 2026 is not locked; if it rises to around £72 an hour the annual cost would breach the board cap, requiring renegotiation or an amended board resolution. The hours are bought perpetually and no one joins the register because of them. The register's downward drift — seven contributors lost since 2024 — is not addressed. And the station remains structurally dependent on a single external supplier for its compliance margin.

None of these is trivial. But the rate risk is manageable (a modest increase still stays near the cap, and the contract is rolling so can be adjusted), and once Local Voice is in payment from April 2027 the board cap lifts. At that point the station has the financial headroom to pursue a coordinator hire alongside or instead of the Halverston contract, achieving the CRANMOOR outcome from a position of greater stability rather than betting the reserve on it.

---

**Summing up**

CRANMOOR is the right destination. ELSWICK is the right route to get there. The February hurdle is real and the consequences of missing it — a prolonged funding gap drawn against a £62,000 reserve — are severe. ELSWICK clears the hurdle with near-certainty, protects the reserve, and preserves the option to build internal capacity once the successor grant is in payment. CRANMOOR asks the station to achieve a recruitment rate it has never approached, in a five-month window, while simultaneously bearing financial exposure it can only partly absorb.

READING

The February measurement requires fourteen hours a week of originated speech, commissioned production below fifty percent of that total, and thirty registered contributors. On contributors both courses are clear; on the commissioned-production ratio ELSWICK (six commissioned out of fifteen total, forty percent) is well inside the rule. The contest is over whether fourteen hours can be reliably reached.

ELSWICK reaches fifteen hours with certainty: nine current hours plus six from Halverston, on a signed contract, starting before the window opens. Cost is £20,280, within the £22,000 board cap even if rates edge up modestly after December 2026; once Local Voice is in payment the annual surplus is around £17,700 and the board cap no longer constrains.

CRANMOOR requires recruiting approximately fifteen active contributors in the five months between coordinator start and measurement. In the whole of 2025 the station added nine contributors without a coordinator — a rate of 0.75 per month. A coordinator could plausibly double that, yielding perhaps nine to ten recruits in the window, likely lifting output to eleven or twelve hours a week rather than fourteen. The station's own planning language ("fourteen hours needs about fifteen more of them") acknowledges the scale of the task. If February is missed, the station enters April 2027 with no grant income, fixed plus coordinator costs of £79,000 a year, and a reserve of roughly £62,000 — potentially losing £26,000 or more before an August reassessment, and still not guaranteed to clear it on the first attempt. A reserve falling to £36,000 is a fragile position for an organisation with £58,000 of immovable annual costs.

CRANMOOR's long-term case is genuine: hours built from the roster cost nothing to repeat, the coordinator tends the register directly, and the structural dependency on Halverston is avoided. But these advantages arrive only if February is cleared, and the probability of clearing it on this timetable against this recruitment history is too low to accept given the financial exposure. Once Local Voice is in payment under ELSWICK the board cap lifts, and a coordinator hire becomes affordable alongside or instead of the Halverston contract — delivering the CRANMOOR outcome from safer ground.

CALL
ELSWICK

GROUNDS
CRANMOOR cannot plausibly recruit the fifteen active contributors it needs within the five months available before the February measurement, and missing that window would expose the reserve to a funding gap the station cannot comfortably absorb, whereas ELSWICK delivers the required hours on contract with near-certainty.
